title: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Elementary Arithmetic” (from p. 117), p. 124. Scope: simple piecewise arithmetic maps on whole numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The trajectories and their sizes are exactly computable, making the finite observational content highly accessible. The asymptotic no-repetition implication and unqualified randomness cannot generally be established by finite runs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Iterate the stated piecewise integer maps from specified seeds and analyze the scalar size series for periodicity, recurrence, entropy rate, autocorrelation, and compression. Irregular size fluctuations over long ranges confirm finite-behavior complexity, whereas a proved cycle would refute the no-repetition component.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No observed repetition over a finite horizon does not prove nonrepetition.

Complex and apparently random are metric-dependent.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The rule and the starting value are explicit, and the quantity plotted is the size of an integer, so the observation is not an artifact of a digit base. Recomputing a long orbit and testing it for repetition is a standard calculation that would confirm the reported complexity or find a cycle that refutes it. The infinite-time reading is stronger than the claim, which is that such rules can produce this behavior.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Iterate n to 5n/2 when n is even and (n+1)/2 when n is odd, starting at 6, and test the logarithmic sizes for a cycle and for autocorrelation. A detected cycle or a simple closed form refutes complex non-repetitive sizes; a very long aperiodic fluctuating orbit confirms the claim for this rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Absence of a cycle in a finite orbit does not prove the orbit never eventually repeats.

Slow growth of the integers makes very long orbits costly, though still routine for millions of steps.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.8
